title: Start Investing Before You Feel Ready
meta_description: See what ten extra compounding years can do, then build a safe early-investing plan using honest assumptions, diversified accounts, automation and low costs.

sections.heading: The Ten-Year Gap Is Time, Not Destiny
paragraphs: A $10,000 investment made at twenty-two has ten more years to compound than the same investment made at thirty-two. That advantage is real, but the familiar comparison often becomes misleading. It assumes both investors choose the same return, pay the same costs, owe no taxes along the way and never withdraw. It can also make a thirty-two-year-old believe the useful window has closed. It has not.

The opening photograph shows a young adult studying market information because an early start is an action, not an age-based trophy. At a hypothetical seven percent annual return, $10,000 invested at twenty-two and left until sixty-five grows to about $183,444. The same amount invested at thirty-two grows to about $93,254. Those are illustrations before inflation, taxes and fees—not forecasts, promises or account statements.

The important feature is not that the first investor earns a magical return. The first dollars complete forty-three compounding periods instead of thirty-three. Returns begin earning returns, but losses compound too, and actual markets arrive in an irregular sequence. A calculator draws a smooth line because it needs a rate; an investor experiences declines, recoveries and uncertainty.

Starting earlier can reduce the monthly amount required for a distant goal, but starting safely matters more than starting recklessly. A young worker with overdue rent, no emergency cash or expensive revolving debt may need stabilization before committing a lump sum to volatile assets. Time is valuable, yet liquidity prevents a forced sale at a bad moment.

Use the age comparison as a lesson in optionality. Early contributions create more years for growth and more opportunities to adjust. Later starters can still build substantial wealth through higher contributions, workplace matches, controlled costs and a plan they can sustain.

Separate the illustration from the decision. The chart answers what happens to one untouched deposit under a constant assumed rate. It does not answer which investment to buy, whether the investor can tolerate loss, or how much retirement will cost. Use the result to value time, then return to present cash flow and risk. If $10,000 is unavailable, do not borrow it merely to match the example. A sequence of smaller contributions can establish the habit without creating a repayment obligation that survives a market decline.

Avoid turning the ages into moral categories. Many people cannot invest at twenty-two because income, family support, disability, education, immigration, housing or debt circumstances differ. The comparison isolates time; it does not measure discipline or worth. Policies, wages and access to workplace plans also shape who can start. A useful guide gives early starters a responsible procedure and later starters a credible recovery path. It never uses a hypothetical balance to shame someone whose earlier dollars were needed for survival, care or a safer future.

sections.heading: Rebuild the Comparison With Visible Assumptions
paragraphs: Every compounding example needs five inputs: starting principal, additional contributions, return assumption, compounding convention and time. It also needs disclosures about fees, taxes and inflation. Change any input and the headline changes. A seven percent nominal illustration is not a claim that a diversified portfolio will earn seven percent every year—or over any particular period.

Calculate with annual periods for a simple classroom comparison, then use monthly deposits for a real contribution plan. Do not quietly compare a twenty-two-year-old who never adds money with a thirty-two-year-old who contributes every month. Answer one question at a time: what does ten extra years do to one deposit, and what ongoing saving could close part of the gap?

Run several rates rather than anchoring on one. At four percent, seven percent and ten percent, the same $10,000 produces very different outcomes. The range shows sensitivity; it does not define a probable corridor. Ten percent is especially unsuitable as a planning guarantee because return and risk are linked and long averages can hide difficult sequences.

Distinguish nominal from real dollars. If prices rise over decades, a future $100,000 will buy less than $100,000 buys today. A real-return illustration subtracts an inflation assumption approximately, while a nominal illustration shows future account dollars. Label the choice and never mix a nominal target with real returns.

The [[S1|Investor.gov compound interest calculator]] can reproduce scenarios, but the quality of the output depends on honest inputs. Save the date and assumptions beside every projection so the number cannot detach from its conditions.

Check the arithmetic independently. Future value for one deposit is principal multiplied by one plus the periodic rate raised to the number of periods. Monthly contributions use a different series because each deposit has a different holding period. Rounding, contribution timing and whether a calculator compounds monthly or annually can explain modest differences between tools. Large differences usually mean an assumption changed. Do not choose the calculator displaying the most attractive result; reconcile inputs until the reason is understood.

sections.heading: Build the Safety Floor Before Market Exposure
paragraphs: An investment horizon is only long when the money can stay invested. Establish a small cash buffer, cover essential bills and prevent foreseeable near-term needs from forcing a withdrawal. The right buffer depends on income stability, insurance, household support, health and upcoming costs. A student with irregular work may need a different reserve from an employee with paid leave and two stable household incomes.

Prioritize employer matching contributions when the plan terms and cash flow permit because the match is compensation, but understand vesting and withdrawal restrictions. Next compare high-cost debt. Paying a credit card charging a high rate produces a certain reduction in interest expense; investing for an uncertain return while revolving that balance often increases risk rather than wealth.

Separate time horizons. Money for rent, tuition, a car next year or an imminent home purchase should not be treated like retirement money merely because stocks have higher long-run expected returns. Use cash or other appropriately stable instruments for near goals. Investment risk should match the date, flexibility and consequence of missing the goal.

Confirm insurance against risks that could erase the plan: health expense, disability, liability and loss of essential property. Investing early while leaving a catastrophic exposure uncovered can make the portfolio a fragile emergency fund.

The safety floor is not an excuse to wait for perfect finances. Define a minimum threshold and a sequence. Someone may make a small matched retirement contribution while building cash and paying expensive debt, then increase investing when the floor is in place.

Write an order of operations for the next dollar. For example: receive the full employer match, maintain the minimum cash reserve, pay required debt minimums, attack identified high-cost balances, then increase diversified long-term investing. Another household may reasonably choose a different order because of job risk or benefits. The value comes from deciding before a market rally or emergency changes emotion. Review the sequence quarterly until the safety floor is complete, then simplify to an annual check.

sections.heading: Choose the Account Before the Investment
paragraphs: An account is a legal and tax container; an investment is what the account owns. A 401(k), IRA and taxable brokerage account can each hold funds, cash or other permitted assets. Opening an IRA does not itself invest the deposit. Confirm that contributions are actually allocated rather than sitting indefinitely in a settlement balance.

Start with a workplace plan when a useful match is available. Review eligibility, vesting, investment menu, administrative fees and Roth or pre-tax options. A match formula may require contributions throughout the year, so front-loading can affect matching unless the plan provides a true-up. Read the plan documents rather than assuming a social-media rule applies.

For 2026, the [[S2|IRS reports]] a $24,500 employee deferral limit for 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457 plans and the Thrift Savings Plan, and a $7,500 IRA contribution limit for those under fifty. These are maximums, not targets or permissions independent of compensation, plan and income rules.

A Roth IRA may provide qualified tax-free withdrawals, while a deductible traditional contribution can reduce current taxable income when eligible. The better choice depends on current and future tax circumstances, access rules and behavior. Avoid presenting “young means Roth” as universal advice.

A taxable account offers flexibility but can generate taxable dividends, interest and realized gains. Tax treatment matters, yet a low-cost diversified investment in an imperfect account can be better than years of paralysis seeking the perfect one.

Confirm withdrawal and transfer rules before funding. Retirement accounts generally carry restrictions and tax consequences that taxable accounts do not; workplace plans can add loan, distribution and spousal-consent provisions. A tax advantage is valuable only when the account fits the goal and the investor can comply with its rules. Keep confirmation statements, contribution totals and tax forms. Accidental excess contributions or an indirect rollover handled incorrectly may require correction, so consult the custodian and a qualified tax professional promptly rather than improvising.

sections.heading: Convert the Goal Into an Automatic Contribution
paragraphs: The original $10,000 may not exist. Replace the intimidating lump sum with a transfer tied to payday. A person investing $100 every two weeks contributes $2,600 in a typical year before growth; increases after raises can matter more than delaying until a five-figure balance appears. Automation turns intention into a repeatable cash-flow decision.

Set the contribution after checking the account limit, employer match and household budget. Schedule the transfer shortly after income arrives, retain a buffer for variable bills and verify the first two deposits. Payroll and brokerage systems can fail because of an election error, bank change or returned transfer. Automation still needs supervision.

Use a contribution escalator. Increase the percentage by one point after a raise, debt payoff or annual review until the target savings rate is reached. Directing part of each raise to investing can raise contributions while preserving some improvement in current life.

Dollar-cost averaging means investing equal amounts at regular intervals regardless of market movement. It can impose discipline, but it does not assure profit or prevent loss. If a lump sum is already available for a long-term goal, delaying solely to wait for a comfortable headline is a separate market-timing decision.

Track contributions separately from investment return. A rising balance during the first years may come mostly from deposits, while a falling market can obscure excellent saving behavior. Reward the controllable process.

If income varies, automate from a conservative base and add a percentage of above-base income after it arrives. A transfer that repeatedly causes overdrafts will be canceled, undermining the habit. Create a minimum, target and stretch contribution so a lean month does not become a total pause. For couples, decide whether targets are household-wide or account-specific and confirm each spouse’s eligibility. Annual limits apply by person or plan category under specific rules, not by the number of accounts opened.

sections.heading: Use Diversification Instead of a Heroic Bet
paragraphs: The midpoint photograph shows market charts and investing tools because execution begins after the account is funded. The age advantage is easily destroyed by concentrating the $10,000 in one company, theme, token or leveraged trade. More time does not make a single security safe. It gives a diversified portfolio more time to experience markets and allows contributions to continue through different conditions.

Diversification spreads exposure across investments, sectors and often regions. The SEC’s [[S3|investor guidance]] explains that diversification can reduce the damage from one holding but cannot prevent broad market losses. A broad mutual fund or exchange-traded fund can simplify diversification, though the fund’s holdings, index, costs and trading structure still require review.

Choose an asset allocation based on horizon, need for return, ability to absorb loss and willingness to stay invested. A young age can support a long horizon, but it does not erase job risk, anxiety or a near-term goal. The portfolio that looks best in a spreadsheet fails if the investor abandons it during an ordinary bear market.

A target-date fund can provide a diversified, changing allocation in one holding. The [[S4|SEC warns]] that funds with the same date can differ in glide path, risk and fees, and the date does not guarantee adequate retirement income. Review whether it is designed to retirement or through retirement.
Write a one-sentence policy naming the account, contribution, allocation and rebalance rule. Simplicity protects attention from becoming speculation.

Look through fund names to underlying holdings. Owning several funds may still create concentration if each holds the same large companies or sector. Conversely, one broad fund can contain thousands of securities. Diversification also includes the investor’s human capital: an employee already dependent on one company for salary and benefits may not want retirement wealth concentrated in employer stock. Review geographic, sector and asset-class exposure at the portfolio level rather than counting ticker symbols.

Diversification must be maintained, not merely purchased once. Contributions and market movement can shift the allocation, while a new fund can duplicate existing exposure. Choose a calendar or percentage-band rebalance method and consider taxes and trading costs before selling in a taxable account. Directing new contributions toward an underweight asset may restore the target with less realization. Rebalancing manages portfolio structure; it does not identify the next market winner. If the desired allocation changes, record the financial reason rather than rewriting history after prices move.

sections.heading: Let Costs Compound Less Than Your Money
paragraphs: Fees reduce the capital that remains available to compound. Compare expense ratios, plan administration charges, advisory fees, trading spreads and account fees. A small percentage applied every year can create a large long-term difference, particularly for an early starter whose holding period is measured in decades.

The SEC’s [[S5|fee bulletin]] illustrates $100,000 growing four percent annually for twenty years: approximately $208,000 with a 0.25 percent annual fee versus about $179,000 with a 1.00 percent fee. The example isolates cost and does not predict returns, but it shows why “only one percent” is not only one percent of the final outcome.

Read the prospectus and plan disclosure rather than relying on a label such as free trading. A zero commission does not eliminate fund expenses, bid-ask spreads, payment conflicts or tax effects. Advisory fees may include useful planning; evaluate the service and total price instead of assuming every fee is waste.

Avoid excessive trading. Taxes, spreads, mistakes and attention can turn a long-horizon plan into a costly reaction loop. Rebalancing at a stated interval or threshold is different from changing strategy because last month’s winner appears exciting.

Review costs annually and after an employer change. Old workplace plans can have favorable institutional pricing or burdensome fees; compare leaving, rolling to a new plan or using an IRA without surrendering protections or triggering tax.

Calculate fees in dollars as well as percentages. Multiply the current balance by the annual rate for a rough first-year figure, then recognize that future balances and fees can change. Ask an adviser what services are included, whether compensation changes by product and how termination works. The cheapest option is not automatically best when it leads to errors or abandonment, but cost must buy identifiable value. Preserve disclosures and compare net-of-fee performance to an appropriate benchmark over a meaningful period.

sections.heading: What the Thirty-Two-Year-Old Can Do Now
paragraphs: Regret is not a contribution. A thirty-two-year-old still has thirty-three years before age sixty-five in the comparison, enough time for deposits and returns to interact powerfully. Begin with today’s cash flow, not a fictional attempt to recreate age twenty-two. Open the appropriate account, capture available match, select a diversified allocation and automate the first sustainable amount.

At a hypothetical seven percent compounded monthly, the future-value gap between the two $10,000 deposits could be offset by about $58 per month from age thirty-two to sixty-five. That illustration assumes every deposit arrives, the return is smooth and fees and taxes are absent. It is useful because the catch-up amount is finite, not because the result is promised.

A later starter may have advantages the early starter lacked: higher income, clearer goals, fewer setup costs or better access to workplace benefits. Convert those advantages into a higher savings rate instead of accepting a permanent label. Use bonuses and raises according to a written allocation rule.

Do not compensate with extreme risk. A concentrated bet cannot reliably replace missing time. Higher expected return generally requires accepting greater uncertainty and loss. Catch up primarily through contributions, expense control, goal flexibility and, when reasonable, a longer earning horizon.
Measure progress against the funded goal, not another person’s birthday. The relevant question is what contribution and allocation make the plan more resilient from this point.

Use a gap analysis rather than a catch-up slogan. Estimate the goal, existing balance, years, conservative return range and planned contributions. Then change controllable inputs one at a time: monthly deposit, retirement date, spending target and account costs. A small adjustment across several levers can be more sustainable than one punishing savings rate. Recalculate annually, not after every market move. The estimate should become more specific as retirement approaches and actual spending history becomes available.

sections.heading: What the Twenty-Two-Year-Old Must Not Assume
paragraphs: Starting young is not permission to neglect everything else. An early investor can still fail through low contributions, panic selling, fraud, leverage, high fees or repeated withdrawals. The first $10,000 matters, but the habit and protection around it matter more. A decade advantage is not a guarantee against poor decisions.

Expect market declines. Before buying, imagine the account at $7,000 and write what you would do. If the money has a distant purpose and the allocation remains appropriate, continued contributions may buy more shares at lower prices. But never promise that recovery will occur by a specific date.

Avoid borrowing to manufacture an early start. Margin and personal loans introduce repayment schedules and the possibility of losses larger than available cash. Employer-plan loans can interrupt compounding and create job-transition complications. Understand every repayment and tax condition before using retirement money.

Protect accounts with unique passwords, multifactor authentication and verified contact information. Name beneficiaries where appropriate and review them after life changes. Ignore unsolicited messages promising certain profits or urgent access to a private opportunity.

The twenty-two-year-old’s real asset is flexibility: the ability to begin small, learn, recover from ordinary mistakes and raise contributions. Preserve that flexibility with low fixed costs and adequate cash.

Early adulthood often contains competing investments in education, relocation, health and career. Not every dollar diverted from a brokerage account is wasted compounding time. Training that safely raises earnings can expand future contributions, while necessary health care protects earning capacity. Compare alternatives without pretending their returns are certain. Keep investing at a sustainable baseline when possible, but do not treat a projection as permission to neglect present safety or an opportunity with strong personal value.

sections.heading: Plan for Interruptions Without Calling the Plan Broken
paragraphs: Caregiving, unemployment, education, illness and housing changes can pause contributions. Model pauses rather than pretending a forty-year plan will be uninterrupted. A contribution holiday reduces the outcome, but it does not erase prior assets or make restarting pointless. Record the restart trigger when the pause begins.

Maintain account records during job changes. Compare leaving assets in the former plan, moving to a new employer plan, completing a direct rollover or using an IRA. A check paid to the worker can create withholding and deadlines; use official instructions and tax advice for the specific transaction.

If an emergency requires a withdrawal, understand tax, penalty and account rules first. Do not let shame delay action on rent, health or safety, but examine alternatives and refill the account deliberately afterward. Retirement accounts are not identical emergency funds.

Update the contribution when income changes. A percentage keeps pace with raises, while a fixed dollar amount may quietly shrink relative to earnings and inflation. During a cut, preserve a token automatic amount if safe because maintaining the process can make recovery easier.
Success is not perfect continuity. It is a system that recognizes interruption, protects essentials and returns to long-term funding without chasing losses.

Model the difference between pausing deposits and withdrawing existing assets. A pause sacrifices new principal and its growth; a withdrawal also removes money already compounding and may add tax or penalty. That distinction supports a separate emergency reserve. When restarting, do not immediately double risk or contributions beyond cash-flow capacity. Restore the old percentage, rebuild reserves and schedule gradual increases. Document any account distribution so tax reporting and basis records remain accurate years later.

sections.heading: Move From Accumulation to a Funded Retirement
paragraphs: The late photograph shows an older couple reviewing documents with an adviser because decades of compounding eventually become decisions about retirement income, taxes, health costs, beneficiaries and withdrawal order. A large balance is not itself a plan. The goal must specify spending, timing, flexibility and risks.

Estimate retirement spending in today’s dollars, include health and housing, and account for Social Security or pension income where applicable. Run more than one lifespan and return sequence. Averages can hide the danger of poor returns near retirement when withdrawals begin.

As the goal approaches, review allocation and capacity for loss. Target-date funds may adjust automatically, but investors should still understand the glide path. Reducing risk does not mean eliminating growth; a retirement lasting decades may still require inflation protection.

Decide when professional help is worth paying for. A fiduciary adviser, tax professional or estate lawyer may add value around retirement transitions, rollovers, concentrated stock, equity compensation or family complexity. Verify credentials, services, compensation and conflicts.

The senior couple is not evidence that early investing guarantees comfort. They represent the destination requiring periodic planning. Every decade should convert the distant goal into more specific decisions.

Retirement planning also needs fraud resistance and custody awareness. SIPC protection at a member brokerage addresses missing cash or securities within statutory limits when a firm fails; it does not protect against market loss, unsuitable advice or an investment declining. Verify a financial professional and firm through official databases, understand where assets are held and review statements directly from the custodian. Never transfer retirement money solely because an unsolicited caller promises safety or unusually consistent returns.

sections.heading: Use a Review Calendar, Not a Market Alarm
paragraphs: Review the plan at least annually and after major life changes. Confirm contribution rate, account limits, beneficiary designations, allocation, fund costs, tax documents and progress toward the goal. Rebalance under the written rule. A review is not a demand to trade; often the correct action is to continue.

Ignore daily performance notifications if they trigger unhelpful changes. Markets provide endless reasons to postpone or panic. A payday contribution and annual review schedule separates the investing process from news intensity.

Keep a projection range showing assumptions, contributions and purchasing-power treatment. Replace old limits with current IRS figures and revise the goal when spending evidence changes. Do not revise expected return upward merely because the required contribution feels uncomfortable.

Use a decision log for material changes: date, reason, alternatives, fees, tax implications and next review. The log exposes repeated performance chasing and helps a future adviser understand the history.

The practical lesson of $10,000 at twenty-two versus thirty-two is neither “you are rich if young” nor “you are late after thirty.” Time has value, contributions have value, costs and risk matter, and the next safe contribution is more useful than regret.

Archive one annual snapshot: balances, contributions, allocation, fees, expected retirement spending, assumptions and action items. The snapshots show whether progress came from saving or markets and make plan drift visible. They also help another trusted person understand the system during incapacity. Remove obsolete accounts from the dashboard only after transfers settle and records are saved. Security alerts deserve immediate attention; performance anxiety does not. Keep those two notification types separate wherever the provider permits.

Finally, test whether the plan can be explained without a spreadsheet. The investor should know why each account exists, what it owns, how much enters, when allocation changes and which event permits a withdrawal. Complexity that cannot be described is difficult to monitor and easy to exploit. Give a trusted contact enough information to locate records without granting unnecessary transaction authority. Review access after marriage, divorce, a move, an employer change or a death. A durable long-term plan combines clear ownership, secure access and behavior that can survive decades of ordinary uncertainty. Run the plan for one month before adding complexity. Confirm the transfer cleared, the cash purchased the intended holding, the fee matched disclosure and the statement reached the correct address. Correct routine failures while balances are small. Reliable operations give compounding time something real to work on throughout the many uncertain years ahead in retirement planning.

summary: Ten extra years can materially change a compounding illustration, but the result depends on principal, contributions, rate, costs, taxes, inflation and uninterrupted time. Treat the age example as a lesson about time, not a command to borrow or speculate. Review it deliberately.

At a hypothetical seven percent annual return, $10,000 at age twenty-two grows to about $183,444 by sixty-five; at thirty-two it grows to about $93,254. Neither amount is promised. Reconcile calculator settings before comparing results from different tools. Review it deliberately.

Use several return assumptions and label nominal versus real dollars. A smooth calculator line does not reproduce actual market sequences. Write the order in which new cash will support safety, debt and investing. Review it deliberately.

Build a safety floor before accepting market risk: essential bills, a cash buffer, high-cost debt review and protection against foreseeable emergencies. Confirm contribution, withdrawal and rollover rules before funding an account. Review it deliberately.

Separate money by horizon. Near-term rent, tuition or home-purchase funds should not be treated like retirement assets. Use minimum, target and stretch contributions when income is irregular. Review it deliberately.

Choose the legal and tax account before selecting its investments. Opening an IRA does not automatically invest the cash deposited. Review underlying holdings because several funds can still own the same securities. Review it deliberately.

For 2026, official limits include $24,500 for employee deferrals to major workplace plans and $7,500 for an IRA for investors under fifty, subject to applicable rules. Translate percentages into dollars and identify what service each recurring fee buys. Review it deliberately.

Capture an employer match when feasible after checking eligibility, vesting, contribution timing and true-up provisions. Change contributions, retirement timing, spending and costs one lever at a time. Review it deliberately.

Automate a sustainable payday contribution and verify that deposits are invested. Increase the percentage after raises or completed debts. Education, health and career spending can also protect or expand future earning capacity. Review it deliberately.

Diversify rather than trying to replace missing time with a concentrated stock, token, sector or leveraged trade. A contribution pause and a withdrawal have different long-term and tax consequences. Review it deliberately.

Match asset allocation to horizon, need, ability to bear loss and willingness to continue—not to age alone. Brokerage-custody protection does not insure investment value or advice quality. Review it deliberately.

Compare recurring fund, plan, advisory and transaction costs. Small annual percentages can create large differences over several decades. Archive an annual snapshot while treating security alerts differently from market noise. Review it deliberately.

A thirty-two-year-old is not too late. At an illustrative seven percent compounded monthly, about $58 monthly could offset the future-value gap in the two $10,000 examples by age sixty-five. Do not increase portfolio risk merely because the projected balance is behind target. Review it deliberately.

A twenty-two-year-old is not guaranteed success. Panic selling, withdrawals, fraud, debt, leverage and high fees can overwhelm the time advantage. Keep records proving contributions, rollovers, cost basis and beneficiary elections. Review it deliberately.

Model contribution pauses for unemployment, caregiving or illness and define a restart trigger instead of declaring the plan broken. Revisit the plan when work, family, health, taxes or the goal materially changes. Review it deliberately.

As retirement approaches, convert balance targets into spending, tax, health, beneficiary and withdrawal decisions. Use current official limits; contribution ceilings and income rules can change annually. Review it deliberately.

Review annually and after life changes. Use a written allocation and rebalance rule instead of reacting to daily market alarms. No calculator can replace a contribution plan the investor can maintain during losses. Review it deliberately.

The next safe contribution matters more than regret about a missed decade or excitement about a projected number. Beginning today is productive at twenty-two, thirty-two and every later workable age. Review it deliberately.

faq.question: Is seven percent a guaranteed investment return?
faq.answer: No. It is an illustrative assumption. Actual returns vary, losses occur, and fees, taxes and inflation change results.

faq.question: Am I too late if I start at thirty-two?
faq.answer: No. Decades may remain. Focus on a sustainable contribution rate, match, diversification, costs and goal flexibility.

faq.question: Should I invest before paying debt?
faq.answer: Compare the debt rate, employer match, liquidity and household risk. High-cost revolving debt often deserves priority while a matched contribution may still be valuable.

faq.question: Does opening an IRA mean my money is invested?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. An IRA is an account container. Confirm that cash is allocated to the intended investment.

faq.question: Is one stock acceptable because I have a long horizon?
faq.answer: A long horizon does not remove company-specific risk. Diversification can reduce concentration risk but cannot prevent broad market loss.

faq.question: Should I invest a lump sum immediately or average in?
faq.answer: The choice depends on horizon, risk and behavior. Regular investing supports discipline; delaying available long-term money is also a market-timing decision.

faq.question: How often should I check my portfolio?
faq.answer: Monitor deposits and security alerts, but use a scheduled annual and life-event review for strategy unless the plan requires a different interval.

glossary.definition: Returns accruing on principal and on prior gains or income left invested.
Growth rate not adjusted for inflation.
Growth after accounting approximately for inflation.
Division of a portfolio among categories such as stocks, bonds and cash.
Spreading exposure to reduce dependence on one holding or risk source.
Annual fund operating expenses expressed as a percentage of assets.
Investing equal amounts at regular intervals regardless of market level.
Diversified fund designed to change its allocation as a named target year approaches.
Process by which an employee gains ownership of employer contributions under plan rules.
Restoring a portfolio toward its intended allocation under a stated rule.
